# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
This is a strong follow-up. It does what the earlier exchange called for: a registered mediation test, a second hours measure, 24-month data, and direct engagement with the comment and the meta-analysis. It also reports reversals honestly, including the termination of the counter arm and the reversions among Halden organisations. Its central conclusion is that the per-hour gain in case-processing declined but persisted at 24 months. That is well supported.

I checked the arithmetic and it holds:

- **Varden per-hour gain:** output per FTE −3.4% with hours −12% (timesheets) gives +9.8%; with hours −11% (logs) it gives +8.5%.
- **Halden continuers:** 96.8 against an hours ratio of 0.866 gives +11.8%.
- **Mediation shares:** 47%, 18% and 35% sum to 100%.

Most of the issues below concern how the new measures are defined, and whether the mediation test is as confirmatory as the summary says.

## 1. What does the system-log hours measure capture?

The logs record "active log-in time on the county's case-management system… time staff are working on cases." That is **time spent on cases**, which is a different thing from total working time. This creates two problems.

- **"Stricter measure" may be the wrong label.** Timesheets record total hours; logs record case time. The two show similar *percentage* changes (−12% and −11%), but "log data show slightly more work than timesheets" compares percentage changes, not levels. Report baseline and month-24 levels on both measures.
- **The mediation result becomes puzzling.** If the outcome is output per hour *of case time*, then cutting meetings does not obviously raise it. Fewer meetings means more case hours, but output per case hour need not change. A 47% mediated share is only plausible if meeting cuts make the case work itself faster, for example through fewer interruptions or longer uninterrupted work. That may well be true, but it is a different mechanism from "removing low-value time." The paper should say which mechanism it means and confirm what the log measure includes.

**A related gap:** if log data exist for the 24-month DiD, they must exist for the pre-period. A 9-month log-based estimate would then give a like-for-like decline on the stricter measure. Its absence from Table 1 needs explaining.

## 2. The mediation test is less confirmatory than the summary claims

- **Timing.** The mediation was registered at month 11, after the exploratory meetings finding and with 11 months of data already collected. If the 24-month analysis uses data from the whole period, it overlaps with the data that generated the hypothesis. A clean confirmatory test would use only months 12–24, or at least report that version as a sensitivity analysis.
- **Effective sample size.** "A larger sample of office-months" overstates the gain. Meeting cuts vary between offices, and there are still only 14 offices. A confidence interval of 28–66% looks narrow for 14 clusters. Say how clustering was handled in the mediation model, for example with a cluster bootstrap.
- **Confounding.** Meeting cuts were not randomised. Offices with more effective managers may both cut meetings more and improve more for other reasons. The limitations section mentions this assumption, but the summary still says "confirms." "Supports" would be accurate.
- **Data source.** The nine-month report said calendar data were collected in month six. This report gives baseline meeting hours (7.4 and 7.2). Say where those came from, for example retrospective calendar extraction, and whether the method matches later measurements.

## 3. The summary mixes measures

The summary says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months." That compares a timesheet figure with a log figure.

- **Like-for-like timesheet figures:** 12.5% falls to 9.8%, a decline of about 22%.
- **Mixed figures:** 12.5% to 8.5% is a decline of about 32%, part of which comes from changing the measure.

The body handles this correctly; the summary and §5 ("about a quarter") should match it. Also, the 9- and 24-month confidence intervals overlap heavily. Test the change formally before describing it as fading. The data are consistent with some decline, but also with none.

## 4. The control-office meeting audit

- **Arithmetic tension.** Two of the seven control offices cut meeting time from 7.1 to 5.0 hours. That alone should lower the control average by about 0.6 hours. Yet the control average moved only from 7.2 to 7.0. The other five offices must therefore have *increased* meetings by around half an hour on average, or the two auditing offices drifted back by month 24. Either is possible, but it should be explained.
- **Contamination.** This is contamination of the control arm and should be named as such. It probably biases the DiD estimate slightly downward, which is conservative. A sensitivity analysis excluding the two offices would show how much.
- **The 4.1% gain.** It compares each office with its own previous six months, so it is exposed to seasonality and regression to the mean. The paper's caveats are appropriate. The closing point is the right one: no arm reorganised without reducing hours, so the trial cannot tell whether the hours cut is necessary or only a trigger. A future trial should include a reorganise-only arm.

## 5. Halden follow-up

- **Baseline hours.** The 40.3-hour baseline is the figure the comment reported for its 27 time-tracking organisations. Is it also these 11 organisations' own baseline? If it was carried over rather than recomputed, the −13.4% and +11.8% figures are unreliable.
- **Non-response.** Of 23 organisations asked, 14 responded. Together with continuation, that adds a third layer of selection, on top of the "survivors twice over" the report already notes.
- **"Upper bound."** The direction is right, but "likely overstates the effect" is safer. Selection is not the only bias at work, and an upper bound is a strong formal claim.
- **The summary's "all with client-facing or coverage obligations."** It stretches the coverage category. A marketing agency citing client deadlines does discretionary work under the meta-analysis's own coding. That is worth stating plainly: some discretionary-work organisations also revert, and their output at reversion (88–91) was well below the continuers'.
- **The Halden withdrawal question.** With a Halden author now a co-author, this report could settle the comment's finding that seven of the nine "preparation-phase" withdrawals happened after the schedule began. A sentence confirming or correcting it would close an open question.

## 6. Smaller points

- **Counter-arm cost.** Restoring output requires 1/0.886, or about 12.9% more staff. That should raise cost per contact by around 12–13%, not 9%, unless non-labour costs make up roughly a quarter of the total. State the assumption.
- **Sick days.** The concern about sick days falling mechanically, raised for the nine-month report, still applies to the −27% figure. Report absence as a share of scheduled hours.
- **Timing of the 24-month estimates.** Say whether the estimates refer to month 24 alone or average over months 13–24. This matters for how the decay is read.
- **§5 on the re-analysis.** This section is fair and well judged. It credits what the comment got right and rejects only the "entirely an artifact" conclusion. One qualification is worth adding: the rebuttal covers public-sector case processing in a single employer.
- **§5 on the meta-analysis.** This is an important finding. It confirms the concern that the four long-follow-up studies were confounded with weak design. The meta-analysis authors should be invited to revise their claim that "novelty can be set aside."

## Overall

Across the five documents, the evidence now points one way:

- In discretionary work, there is a real per-hour gain of roughly 8–10% under good measurement. It fades somewhat over two years and is partly explained by organisational changes such as cutting meetings, not just by rest.
- In coverage-bound work, output and service fall unless more staff are hired.

This report is the most credible single source for that conclusion. The fixes that matter most:

1. Clarify what the log measure captures.
2. Rerun the mediation on post-registration data, with clustering accounted for.
3. Use like-for-like figures in the summary.
4. Explain the control-office meeting arithmetic.
